course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Measurements
unit.blurb: Why scientists measure, SI units, and how to measure length, area, volume, mass and time accurately – avoiding parallax errors and outliers.

O1.t: Distinguish qualitative and quantitative observations and name SI units for physical quantities.

O2.t: Measure length with suitable instruments, convert units and avoid parallax error.

O3.t: Repeat measurements, spot outliers, calculate averages and explain accuracy and precision.

O4.t: Calculate area (base × height) and convert units of area.

O5.t: Measure volume with a measuring cylinder (meniscus) and by displacement; convert units of volume.

O6.t: Measure mass with a balance, using tare, and convert units of mass.

O7.t: Measure time intervals and convert units of time.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 2: Measurements.
Today we will learn why scientists measure things, which units they use,
and how to measure length, area, volume, mass and time accurately.
How can a running track be exactly the same length all around the world?
And how do we measure the tiny differences in time that decide a world record,
or the height of a high jump?
Measurements must be made in standard units.
Otherwise we could never compare athletes from different countries,
and there would be no world records.
Measurement also helps us look after our planet.
Scientists measure air quality, water pollution and animal populations to protect the environment.
Measurements are not just for scientists.
Let's see four people who measure every day, and the units they use.
A pharmacist measures five millilitres of medicine for a child.
Too much could be dangerous, so the volume must be exact.
A baker weighs two hundred and fifty grams of flour.
Mass is measured in grams and kilograms.
A nurse measures a temperature of thirty-eight point five degrees Celsius.
That is a fever, so the patient needs care.
A race official times a sprint at ten point five two seconds.
Time is measured in seconds.
Every measurement is a number and a unit.
Pause and decide: which of these four measurements is already given in an SI unit?
Look at this runner.
How fast is she really running?
How could we find out?
If we say “she runs fast”, we are making a qualitative observation.
It is described in words.
If we measure that she runs 100 metres in 14.2 seconds,
we are making a quantitative observation.
It uses numbers.
We use instruments to make quantitative observations.
That makes them objective: based on facts, not opinions.
Long ago, people measured with parts of their bodies.
A cubit was the length from the elbow to the tip of the longest finger.
But people's arms are not all the same size!
So people began to use sticks and pieces of string marked with standard lengths.
In 1875, scientists agreed to define the metre using a
special bar made of a hard platinum and iridium alloy,
which does not rust or scratch easily.
It was kept locked away in Paris.
Today we use modern instruments, like tape measures, electronic balances, stopwatches and thermometers,
to make accurate measurements.
Length is a physical quantity:
something in the physical world that can be measured.
Mass, time and temperature are physical quantities too.
Scientists around the world have agreed on standard units for each quantity,
called SI units. Length is measured in metres and mass in kilograms.
Time is measured in seconds, temperature in kelvin, and electric current in amperes.

captions: Length is the distance between two points.
Height and diameter are lengths too.
The SI unit of length is the metre.
For very large or very small lengths we use prefixes.
Kilo means a thousand, so a kilometre is a thousand metres.
Milli means one thousandth, so a millimetre is a thousandth of a metre.
To change a big unit into a smaller one, we multiply.
To change a small unit into a bigger one, we divide.
So: one kilometre is 1000 metres, one metre is 100 centimetres,
and one centimetre is 10 millimetres.
The instrument must match the job.
We use a metre rule for longer lengths, like a piece of wood,
and a 30 centimetre rule for small objects like a book or a pen.
A soft tape measure wraps around curved things like your waist.
A hard tape measure is good for rooms and furniture.
Vernier calipers measure very small lengths,
such as the width of a pin or the size of a bolt.
For big distances we use a measuring wheel for a sports field,
an odometer for the distance a car travels, and a theodolite,
which surveyors use to measure distances and angles.
To measure length with a rule,
first line up one end of the object with the zero mark.
If you read the scale from an angle, from position A or C,
you get the wrong reading: 19.8 or 20.2 centimetres.
Put your eye directly above the mark, at position B,
and you read the correct value: 20.0 centimetres.
Reading from the wrong angle is called a parallax error.
Always look vertically down at the mark.
A single sheet of paper is too thin to measure with a ruler.
Predict: how could you find its thickness using a ruler?
Pause and think of a method.
Watch. Instead of one sheet,
we take one hundred identical sheets from the same book.
We press them together and measure the whole stack with a ruler.
It is 8 millimetres thick.
Now we divide: 8 millimetres divided by 100 gives 0.08 millimetres for one sheet.
Explain the method. Measuring many sheets makes the
length big enough to read on the ruler,
and dividing shares it equally between the sheets.
Any small reading error is also divided by 100,
so the answer is more accurate.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
How can you tell if a measurement is accurate?
First, ask if it is reasonable.
A paper clip 26.8 centimetres long?
That can't be right, so measure again.
Always repeat measurements. Three measurements are enough if
at least two of them are close together.
Close results are precise.
Leave out any obviously wrong result, called an outlier, and calculate the average.
For clip X, 3.2 plus 3.0, divided by 2, gives 3.1 centimetres.
If other people repeat the measurement and get the same results,
our results are reliable.
Accuracy and precision are not the same.
Here, every dart is close to the centre and close together:
high accuracy and high precision.
Here, the darts are close together but far from the centre:
precise but not accurate.
These darts are spread out.
On the left they average near the centre,
but on the right they are neither accurate nor precise.
Remember: accurate means close to the true value,
and precise means close to one another.
Darts that land close together but away from the target are precise,
but not accurate.

captions: Area is the amount of space taken up by a flat, two-dimensional surface.
The SI unit is the square metre.
This mosaic is made of small tiles, each 1 centimetre by 1 centimetre,

Ten rows of ten tiles make 100 tiles,

A tile 12 centimetres long and 7 centimetres high has 12 times 7,

So for a rectangle, area equals base times height.
To convert units of area, square the length factor.
Since 1 metre is 100 centimetres, 1 square metre is 100 times 100,
which is 10,000 square centimetres.
A leaf is not a rectangle, so we cannot use base times height.

There are 20.

There are 12. Squares less than half covered are ignored.
Add them together: 20 plus 12 gives about 32 square centimetres.
Explain why this works.
Each square has an area of one square centimetre.
Counting a square when more than half of it is covered,
and ignoring it when less than half is covered, balances out the edges.
Smaller squares would give a more accurate answer.

q.prompt: 38 cm³ → 49 cm³. Stone volume?

captions: Volume is the amount of space taken up by an object or a substance.
The SI unit is the cubic metre,
but a cubic metre is very big!
So we often use smaller units: the cubic centimetre,
the litre and the millilitre.
One litre is a thousand millilitres,
which is the same as a thousand cubic centimetres.
So one millilitre equals one cubic centimetre.
Volumes in everyday life range from tiny to enormous.
Let's compare four of them.
A medicine spoon holds five millilitres,
which is the same as five cubic centimetres.
A can of drink holds three hundred and thirty millilitres.
A large water bottle holds one and a half litres,
which is fifteen hundred millilitres.
An Olympic swimming pool holds about two and a half million litres.
That is two thousand five hundred cubic metres!
Remember: one litre is a thousand millilitres.
Pause and work out:
how many medicine spoons of five millilitres would fill the large bottle?
We measure the volume of a liquid with a measuring cylinder.
Look closely: the surface of the water curves up where it touches the glass.
If your eye is too high or too low,
you will make a parallax error and read the wrong volume.
Put your eye level with the surface of the liquid.
The curved surface is called the meniscus.
For an accurate reading, read the level at the bottom of the meniscus.
How do we find the volume of an irregular object, like a stone?
We can't use a formula, so we use the displacement method.
First, pour some water into a measuring cylinder and record the starting volume:
38 cubic centimetres.
Then carefully lower the stone into the water on a string.
The water level rises to 49 cubic centimetres.
Subtract: 49 minus 38 equals 11.
The volume of the stone is 11 cubic centimetres,
because it pushed aside its own volume of water.

captions: The mass of an object is the amount of matter in it.
The SI unit is the kilogram.
Smaller masses are measured in grams and milligrams.
One kilogram is 1000 grams, and one gram is 1000 milligrams.
A feather has a mass of only about 0.008 grams,
while a cat has a mass of about 3 to 5 kilograms.
What about your suitcase at the airport?
Its mass is measured in kilograms.
We measure mass with a balance.
There are beam balances and electronic balances.
Always start by setting the reading to zero.
Often we don't want to include the mass of the container.
Put the empty beaker on the balance first.
Then press the tare button.
The reading goes back to zero.
Now add the substance.
The balance shows only the mass of the substance: 25 grams.
A dish of ice cubes sits on an electronic balance.
It reads one hundred and fifty grams.
Predict: when all the ice has melted, will the reading go up,
go down, or stay the same?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The ice slowly melts in the warm room.
After thirty minutes all the ice has turned into water.
The balance still reads one hundred and fifty grams.
Explain what you saw.
Melting changes ice into liquid water,
but no matter is added or taken away.
The amount of matter, its mass, stays the same.
Only the volume and shape change.
Pause and explain it in your own words.

captions: The SI unit of time is the second.
We also use minutes and hours: one hour is 60 minutes,
and one minute is 60 seconds.
Over the centuries people have measured time in many ways,
for example with sundials and hourglasses.
Today clocks, watches and smartphones keep track of the time of day.
To measure a time interval,
such as how long an object takes to travel a distance,
we use a stopwatch or a laboratory timer.
A partner holds a ruler and drops it without warning.
You catch it as fast as you can.
The shorter the distance it falls, the faster your reaction.
Here are five trials from one student, in centimetres.
Trial 3 is much longer than the others.
It is an outlier.
Perhaps the student was not looking.
Pause and work out the mean of the other four trials.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Convert 2.5 km into metres.
Pause the video now.
Question 2: What is the bottom of the curved liquid surface called,
and why do we read it at eye level?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The meniscus – reading at eye level avoids a parallax error.
Question 3: Water rises from 30 cm³ to 42 cm³ when a stone is added.
What is the stone's volume?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 42 − 30 = 12 cm³.
Question 4: Darts land close together but far from the target.
Accurate or precise? Pause the video now.
Answer: Precise but not accurate.
